hints: Focus on what 'single substance' really means here, that both a different atom arrangement and a different 3D arrangement would count as a different substance.
Look for hidden stereochemistry first, check option A for four different groups on one carbon and option B for a C=C that can be cis and trans.
Now compare a condensed structural formula that fixes all connections with a molecular formula like C4H10, and ask which one leaves no room for any other isomer.
walkthrough:
**Understand the test**

A single substance means the formula must allow only one structural isomer AND only one stereoisomer. Remember to check for chain or positional isomerism, for E/Z isomerism at C=C, and for optical isomerism at a chiral centre.

Rule to use:
$$\text{chiral centre = carbon with 4 different groups}$$

**Check A for optical isomerism**

Look at $\text{CH}_3\text{CHClCH}_2\text{CHO}$, which is 3-chlorobutanal. The second carbon is bonded to $\text{CH}_3$, H, Cl and $\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$, four different groups.

So it is chiral and exists as a pair of enantiomers, not a single substance.

**Check B for geometric isomerism**

$\text{CH}_3\text{CHCHCH}_3$ represents but-2-ene, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHCH}_3$. A C=C with two different groups on each end shows cis-trans (E/Z) isomerism.

So B represents two stereoisomers, not a single substance.

**Check D for structural isomerism**

$\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}$ is only a molecular formula. It can be arranged as straight chain butane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, or branched methylpropane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CH}_3$.

So D represents two structural isomers.

**Confirm C is unique**

$\text{CH}_2\text{ClCH}_2\text{CHCl}_2$ fixes the exact connectivity: 1,1,3-trichloropropane. Carbon 1 has two H atoms and carbon 3 has two Cl atoms, so neither is chiral, and there is no C=C.

No structural rearrangement is possible without changing the formula, and no stereoisomer exists, so this identifies a single substance.

options.A: Incorrect. $\text{CH}_3\text{CHClCH}_2\text{CHO}$ has a chiral centre at the CHCl carbon, bonded to H, Cl, $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$. It therefore exists as two optical isomers (enantiomers), so it does not identify a single substance.
options.B: Incorrect. $\text{CH}_3\text{CHCHCH}_3$ is but-2-ene, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHCH}_3$. The double bond allows cis and trans (E and Z) stereoisomers, so this formula covers two different substances.
options.C: Correct. $\text{CH}_2\text{ClCH}_2\text{CHCl}_2$ shows the full carbon skeleton and positions of the Cl atoms. There is no C=C for E/Z isomerism and no carbon with four different groups for optical isomerism, so only one substance is possible.
options.D: Incorrect. $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}$ is a molecular formula shared by two structural isomers, n-butane and 2-methylpropane. Many students forget that a molecular formula alone rarely identifies a single alkane beyond C3.
